To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the health sector in Africa is not performing well, that it is performing poorly because it is not allocating resources optimally and not using them efficiently, and that it could perform much better if the right policies and interventions were put into place.

the health status maximization of individuals, as an appropriate social objective, can be measured by the disability-adjusted life years lost, that the market fails to deliver this objective, and that the most promising interventions to improve performance are those addressing knowledge gaps and those addressing institutional failures.
the disability-adjusted life years lost is a feasible measure of health and that the health status maximization criterion provides a useful analytical basis for health sector reform.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have made a start in the analytical approach to health reform, but there is a long way to go.
we now know a lot more about what to do, and how to do it, to reform the health sector in developing countries.
we now have the tools for an analytical approach to reform.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be much more explicit about our objectives for health sector reform and about the information we need to achieve these objectives.
health sector reform is not just a set of ad hoc policy changes.

health sector reform is a complex and multifaceted undertaking that needs to be based on a clear understanding of the nature of health sector market failures and a clear definition of the objectives and priorities for health sector reform.
